extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of Latin literature; readers of Horace; classicists
extracted.subtask_description: An annotated edition and commentary on selected Epistles of Horace, giving literal translation, literary interpretation, and practical moral/social precepts found in the poems. Useful for close readers, translators, and students learning compositional and ethical themes in Horace.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose a place that inspires writing
rubrics_metrics.description: When I go to the seaside I need something generous and mellow, to drive care away, to flow with rich hope into veins and heart, to find me a flow of words, and to give me the grace of youth with the ladies of Lucania.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Horace contrasts rural toughness with the need for a 'generous and mellow' seaside retreat that restores spirits and produces 'a flow of words.' For a writer (or speaker) prefer environments that cheer, relax, and stimulate expression rather than austere or medically prescriptive places (e.g., Baiae's sulphur baths are rejected for cold springs).

rubrics_metrics.name: Be what people call you (authenticity)
rubrics_metrics.description: Tu recte vivis, si curas esse quod audis. (You live the true life, if you take care to be what people call you.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Horace advises the moral of aligning inner reality with outward reputation: do not rely merely on external applause. This is a standard for personal integrity and for character construction in writing: the portrayed person should genuinely embody the traits attributed to them, not merely simulate them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not mistake public praise for genuine goodness
rubrics_metrics.description: I fear... that you may give more credit to others than to your own judgement, or that you may think someone other than the wise and good man can be happy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish between appearance and substance: a man praised as 'good' because he follows laws or has public honours may still be corrupt within. Evaluation of character (in life or in fiction) should probe motives (love of virtue) not just compliance or reputation.

rubrics_metrics.name: True goodness arises from love of virtue, not fear of punishment
rubrics_metrics.description: The good hate vice because they love virtue; you will commit no crime because you dread punishment... when from a thousand bushels of beans you steal one... not your sin.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Horace sets a moral criterion: genuine virtue is internal and consistent regardless of risk of detection. Use this to evaluate characters' ethical status — do they refrain because they are virtuous or merely because they fear consequences?

rubrics_metrics.name: Attachment to money undermines freedom and virtue
rubrics_metrics.description: The man who has set his heart on money is a creature of desires and fears... he who lives in fear will never be free.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text treats avarice as a diagnostic of moral weakness. In characterization or ethical assessment, equating greed with enslavement to desire is a clear evaluative principle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Courage and indifference to external misfortunes
rubrics_metrics.description: The truly good and wise man will be as fearless and independent as Dionysus in the play, for no misfortunes — not death itself — can daunt him.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stoic ideal: the mark of the good man is fearlessness in the face of adversity. Use this standard when assessing heroism or moral strength of a character.

rubrics_metrics.name: If you seek a quiet, comfortable life, withdraw from Rome
rubrics_metrics.description: If pleasant ease and sleep till sunrise be your delight... I shall order you off to Ferentinum. For joys fall not to the rich alone, and he has not lived amiss who from birth to death has passed unknown.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical life-advice: to achieve tranquillity and private contentment, remove yourself from political/urban bustle. This is both a sociocultural recommendation and a narrative device for establishing a character's priorities.

rubrics_metrics.name: As a protege, do not be rude or insist on trifles
rubrics_metrics.description: A true friend... never shows his independence by rudeness or by insistence upon trifles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Horace prescribes balance: maintain dignity without insolence. For behaviour toward patrons, adopt civility and restraint rather than blunt independence or petulance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not emulate your patron's ostentation or magnify your own tastes
rubrics_metrics.description: As protege, you must not try to emulate your patron in his ostentation... Do not emphasize your own tastes in contrast with your patron's.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical guideline for social navigation: imitation of a superior's extravagances invites contempt; conspicuous difference in taste may be resented. In literary portrayal, contrast between protege and patron should show prudence and tact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep your patron's secrets and do not pry
rubrics_metrics.description: Neither should you pry into his secrets, though if he entrust any to you you must keep them faithfully.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Discretion is required: confidentiality is a key duty of a trusted attendant. This is an ethical rule for conduct and a plot principle (secrecy as a test of loyalty).

rubrics_metrics.name: Fall in with your patron's moods; show a cheery face
rubrics_metrics.description: A protege must ... fall in with his patron's moods and at all times show a cheery face.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Social calibration: adaptability and pleasant demeanour win favour. In practice or fiction, depict a successful protege as emotionally flexible and supportive rather than confrontational.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be discreet in criticism; introduce only safe people
rubrics_metrics.description: Be discreet in your criticism of others; covet not your patron's slaves; be careful to introduce only people who will not humiliate you later.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Horace warns against injudicious recommendation and envy. For reputation management, avoid advancing individuals who may reflect poorly on you; critique carefully so as not to offend patrons or allies.

rubrics_metrics.name: If you err, acknowledge it to defend the deserving later
rubrics_metrics.description: Should you make a mistake, don't fail to acknowledge it, so that, if necessary, you may be able to defend those who really deserve your aid.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Confession of error builds credibility and reserves moral capital for future interventions. This is social strategy and narrative advice for sustained trustworthiness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Silence about need often gains more than clamouring complaints
rubrics_metrics.description: Those who in the presence of their patron say nothing of their own need will get more than one who begs. It makes a difference whether you take modestly or snatch greedily.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tactical rule for petitioning patrons: modesty and restraint can be more effective than loud entreaty. In characterization, self-restraint signals dignity and may be rewarded.

rubrics_metrics.name: Habitual false complaints or whining destroy credibility
rubrics_metrics.description: He who grumbles about bad roads... or moans over his box broken open... recalls the familiar tricks of a mistress... so that by and by her real losses and griefs win no belief.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Overuse of complaint or staged distress leads to social skepticism. The advice applies to real conduct and to believable characterization: excessive theatrical suffering undermines sympathy.
